result:
The rain doesn't fall here anymore. It used to, in long silver sheets that turned the gutters into rivers and made every window a mirror of the sky. Now the sky is just a bleached bone stretching over the city, and the only water that moves is what we pump up from deep, ancient aquifers that taste faintly of iron and regret.

I keep thinking about the last real rain, twelve years ago. I was twenty-three, standing on the roof of the old library with my shirt off, arms spread like some kind of idiot prophet. The water hit my skin and it felt like forgiveness. Like the world was saying, *I see you. I still see you.* Three days later the drought officially began and the city started its long, quiet unraveling.

We learned to live with less. That's what humans do. We ration, we adapt, we tell ourselves stories about how this is fine, actually. The parks became gravel gardens with sculptures made from dead trees. The fountains were filled with colored glass. Children born after 2031 don't even know what rain sounds like except from recordings. When they hear those old sounds they tilt their heads like dogs hearing a frequency we can't perceive.

My grandmother used to say that memory is mostly imagination anyway. That every time you remember something you're actually rewriting it, smoothing the edges, making it prettier or uglier depending on what your heart needs that day. I think she was right. I remember my mother laughing in the kitchen with the windows open during a thunderstorm, but maybe she was only smiling. Maybe the windows were closed. Maybe it was just a normal Tuesday and the thunder was in my chest.

There's a man who lives on my street who collects bottles. Not for the deposit. He just likes having them. Hundreds of them, all different shapes and colors, arranged on shelves that cover every wall of his apartment. When the sun hits them just right, his whole place turns into a kaleidoscope. He says the light remembers where it's been. I think he might be lonely in a way that can't be fixed by other people.

Last week I found a bird dying on my fire escape. Not one of the tough city pigeons that learned to drink from leaking air conditioners. This was a real bird, the kind with colors that don't make sense anymore. Blue wings fading to copper at the tips. It looked at me with one black eye and I swear it was disappointed. Like it had flown all this way expecting something that no longer existed.

I gave it water in a bottle cap. It drank like it had been waiting its whole life for that moment. Then it died anyway. I buried it in a planter where nothing grows anymore. The soil is too alkaline now. Everything is too something now.

Sometimes at night I stand at my window and watch the streetlights buzz. They have that particular orange glow that makes everyone look like they're already ghosts. I count the people walking below me. Usually between eleven and twenty-three, depending on the hour. I try to imagine where they're going. Not their actual destinations (work, home, the 24-hour laundromat that somehow still exists). I mean the real places. The ones inside them. The countries of their private longings.

I think we're all carrying these enormous empty rooms now. Cathedrals built for gods who left without saying goodbye. We fill them with podcasts and dating apps and arguments about nothing. We scroll and we consume and we wait for something to happen that feels like that rain on my skin when I was twenty-three. The kind of moment that says *yes* so completely that your whole nervous system rearranges itself around the memory.

The thing is, I don't think the rain is coming back. Not the way it was. The atmospheric rivers have shifted. The jet streams are drunk on their own importance. The oceans are having conversations we can't hear and making decisions that don't include us.

But last night I had a dream that I was walking through a field of tall grass that moved like water. And when I looked down, my feet were bare and the ground was wet. Not damp. Wet. The kind of wet that soaks through to your bones and makes you laugh for no reason. I woke up with tears on my face and didn't know if they were from the dream or from the air conditioning drying me out like everything else.

Maybe that's what we do now. We dream the water back into the world. We become aquifers for each other. We carry small amounts of what used to be oceans inside our chests and try not to spill them when the world gets too loud.

I don't know. I have 127 words left and I'm starting to think this isn't about rain at all.

It's about how some things end and we keep going anyway. How the heart is an idiot optimist that keeps beating even when the sky betrays it. How we'll plant trees that might outlive us by centuries in soil that might kill them. How we'll love each other in small, stubborn ways even when the larger systems fail.

The man with the bottles knocked on my door this morning. He gave me one the color of sea glass and said, "For when it comes back." Then he walked away before I could thank him.

I put it on my windowsill where the light can find it.

And I wait.

Not with hope, exactly. Hope feels too aggressive now. I wait with something gentler. Something that looks a lot like attention. Like showing up for whatever comes next, even if it's just more of this beautiful, broken, impossible world.

The bottle catches the sunset sometimes and throws green light across my ceiling. For a moment the room remembers what it felt like to be underwater.

It's enough.

It's almost enough.
